title: Gnocchi alla Romana
subtitle: Baked semolina gnocchi with butter and Parmesan
excerpt: Gnocchi alla romana are round discs of semolina porridge, enriched with butter, Parmesan, and egg yolk, then baked until golden and crisp on top. They are entirely different from potato gnocchi: more substantial, with a firm, creamy interior and a crunchy crust. They are a Roman classic and one of the easiest gnocchi to make.
sourceNotes: Gnocchi alla romana are a traditional Roman dish, quite different from the potato gnocchi of northern Italy. Made from semolino (coarse semolina) cooked in milk, they appear in Artusi (1891) and in Pellegrino Artusi's and Ada Boni's Roman cookery texts.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the semolina sheet the day before and refrigerate. Stamp out, top, and bake on the day.

content.text: Gnocchi alla romana are made in two stages: first the semolina porridge is made and spread into a thin sheet to set, then rounds are stamped out, overlapped in a dish, topped with butter and Parmesan, and baked. The resting time is essential -- the porridge must be completely set and cold before the rounds are cut.

Bring {{whole-milk}} milk to a gentle simmer in a large saucepan with {{salt-table}} salt. Pour in {{semolina}} semolina in a thin stream, whisking constantly to avoid lumps. Switch to a wooden spoon and stir over medium heat for 10 to 12 minutes until the porridge is very thick and pulls away from the sides of the pan.

Remove from the heat. Beat in {{unsalted-butter}} butter, {{parmesan}} Parmesan, {{egg-yolks}} egg yolks, and {{nutmeg}} nutmeg. Pour onto a clean, wet baking tray and spread to about 1.5cm thick. Leave to cool and set for at least 1 hour (or overnight in the fridge).

Preheat the oven to 200C. Stamp out rounds from the set semolina using a 6cm pastry cutter dipped in water. Overlap them in a buttered baking dish. Brush with the melted {{unsalted-butter}} butter and dust with {{parmesan}} Parmesan. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until deep golden and crisp on top. Serve from the dish.

items.cause: The semolina was added too quickly or the milk was too cold.
items.fix: Bring the milk to a full simmer before adding the semolina, and add it in a thin, slow stream while whisking. If lumps form, press them against the side of the pan with a wooden spoon.

content.text: Gnocchi alla romana are a Thursday dish in Rome, as potato gnocchi are in Venice. They are found on the menus of Roman trattorie alongside the other Thursday classic, coda alla vaccinara. The dish is made from pantry ingredients and requires no pasta machine or potato ricer. It is one of the most practical and satisfying dishes in the Roman canon, and it reheats well the next day.
